title: Empengyere
author: Kaaka Kyomuhendo
desc: Whole maize boiled about eight hours in a clay pot until it finally goes tender, then beans added, with stinging nettle and pumpkin leaves — served with pumpkin and obushera.
longDesc: Empengyere is whole maize and beans cooked in a clay pot, and the eight hours are not an exaggeration: whole dried maize kernels take that long to become tender, and nothing shortens it. The beans go in afterwards, and the greens are stinging nettle and pumpkin leaves. It belongs to the Bakiga of Kabale, Rukiga, Kanungu and Rukungiri, and it is served with pumpkin and a cup of obushera — which makes it one of the most complete single meals in the country.
equipment: Clay pot, or a heavy pot
steps: Soak the maize and the beans separately overnight.
Boil the whole maize in a clay pot for about eight hours, until tender. Top up the water as it reduces.
Add the beans and continue cooking until they are soft.
Add the stinging nettle and pumpkin leaves.
chefTips: About eight hours for the maize, and there is no way round it. Whole dried kernels are the hardest thing to cook in a Ugandan kitchen and this dish is defined by the patience it takes.
Beans after the maize, not with it. Beans cooked for eight hours disintegrate entirely.
Top the water up throughout. Eight hours will empty any pot.
A clay pot is specified and it does hold a low even heat better than metal over a fire. A heavy pot is the substitute.
Handle the stinging nettle with gloves until it is in the pot. Cooking destroys the sting completely.
Nettle is a real vegetable here rather than a foraged curiosity — high in iron and protein and eaten deliberately.
Served with pumpkin and obushera, it is a full meal: grain, pulse, greens, a vegetable and a fermented drink.
No quantities are documented. The one source is a named Ugandan journalist and it gives none, so nothing here is estimated.
commonMistakes: Adding the beans at the start.
Adding the greens hours before serving.
sources: Adapted from Grace Musiimenta, 'Food culture: Bakiga empengyere redefining Uganda's traditional cuisine', Nexus Media, 2025 — the maize boiled about eight hours until tender, the beans added afterwards, the stinging nettle and pumpkin leaves, the clay pots, the service with pumpkin and obushera, and the districts of Kabale, Rukiga, Kanungu and Rukungiri are all from that article. It is by a named Ugandan journalist, it gives no quantities, and it is the only source on this dish.
No quantities have been estimated. The overnight soaking of the maize and beans is standard practice for both and is not stated in that source.
Obushera, the accompanying drink, appears in this collection as UGA085.
storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days. It is better the next day.
reheating: Warm gently with a little water.
healthBenefits: Maize and beans together form a complete protein.
Stinging nettle is exceptionally high in iron, calcium and protein for a leaf.
Pumpkin leaves add vitamin A, iron and folate.
Very high in fibre, and cooked with no added fat at all.
culturalNote: An eight-hour dish tells you about a household as much as a recipe: a fire that stays lit, someone at home, and a pot that can be left. Kigezi is cold, hilly and hungry country, and empengyere is the answer to all three at once.
